title: Sherpa Tensing — Descent Three: Past Simple Passive (B1)
description: Coming down, the same tenses are lit from the other side. The passive keeps the event and lets the doer go — because you do not know who, or it does not…

hero.lede: Coming down, the same tenses are lit from the other side. The passive keeps the event and lets the doer go — because you do not know who, or it does not matter, or you would rather not say. Same past simple, same place on the line, different subject.

sections.label: Descent briefing
sections.title: When to use it
sections.lead: The passive is not a different tense. It is the same past simple with the doer let go — and the reason you let them go is always one of these six.

cards.head: You do not know who
cards.body: Nobody can tell you the doer, so the sentence does without one.

cards.head: The doer does not matter
cards.body: The event is the news; who did it is a footnote.

cards.head: The doer is obvious
cards.body: Saying it would be a waste of everyone's time.

cards.head: You would rather not say
cards.body: The most quietly political sentence in English does exactly this.

cards.head: Putting the important thing first
cards.body: English gives the front of the sentence to what the sentence is about.

cards.head: Putting the doer back with by
cards.body: When the doer is the point, it goes at the end, where the weight falls.

charts.head: Turning an active sentence around
charts.note: Three moves, always in the same order: the object comes to the front, the verb becomes was/were + participle, and the old subject either disappears or goes to the back behind by.

head: Active
Passive
What moved
rows: The roof came first; the storm went.
The bridge was built by Brunel.
Brunel matters, so he stayed — at the end.

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: Only be changes, exactly as it does in camp three: was for I, he, she and it; were for the rest. The participle never moves.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with the passive is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: After be comes the third form, never the infinitive or the past simple.
Verbs with no object have no passive — happen, arrive, die, exist, seem.
The bridge was built from Brunel.
The bridge was built by Brunel.
The doer takes by. With is for the instrument: cut with a knife.

charts.note: Neither is better. The question is only what the sentence is about — because whatever you put at the front is what the reader will think it is about.

head: Question
Passive
Active
rows:
The thing it happened to.
"The roof was damaged."

The one who did it.
"The storm damaged the roof."
Often not — and you do not need to.
Yes, and you are naming them.
At the end with by, or nowhere at all.
At the front, as the subject.
Longer by two or three words.
Usually shorter. Prefer it when both work.

charts.example: The pair worth remembering: "I made a mistake" and "A mistake was made" say the same thing about the world and completely different things about the speaker. That choice is the passive's real power, and the reason to know when someone is using it on you.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Reach for the passive when
items: a report or notice needs distance

signals.head: Verbs with no passive at all

sections.example: The test for whether a verb can go passive: does it take an object? They built it has one, so it turns. It happened has none, so it cannot.

sections.label: Interactive
sections.title: The event, and the doer you dropped

diagram.intro: The block is the same past simple block as the ascent, lit from above instead of fading into the dark — because the tense has not changed, only the light. Inside it sits a dashed box: the doer. It is drawn inside the event rather than beside it because the doer is not a moment in time, it is a part of the sentence — and it is dashed because most of the time nobody says it. Click either to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: The event — now the subject
items: The window was broken during the night.

panels.head: The doer — optional, and usually gone
items: … and most of the time, nothing at all.

quiz.explain: Was + the third form: was broken. Break / broke / broken.

quiz.hint: The date is the news, not the builder.
quiz.explain: The participle of build is built, and the singular subject takes was.
Villages is plural, so were, and the participle takes -ed: were evacuated.

quiz.hint: The doer is the point here.
quiz.explain: The doer goes at the end behind by, and the participle of write is written.

quiz.prompt: The forms _____ , so the claim failed. (not / sign)
quiz.explain: Weren't + participle. The plural forms takes were.
Questions invert be: Was the roof damaged? Roof is singular.

quiz.prompt: It _____ last night, and nobody saw it coming. (happen)
quiz.explain: Happen takes no object, so it has no passive. It happened.

quiz.prompt: The trains _____ because of the ice. (cancel)
quiz.hint: Plural, and no doer worth naming.
quiz.explain: Trains is plural, so were cancelled. Who cancelled them adds nothing.
By the police goes without saying, so the passive drops it.
Steal / stole / stolen. Someone stole my bike carries no information, so the passive is better.
The doer of a passive takes by. With is for the instrument: cut with a knife.

quiz.prompt: We _____ nothing about the change until Friday. (tell)
quiz.explain: We is plural, so were, and the participle of tell is told.

quiz.prompt: A mistake _____ , and the letter went out anyway. (make)
quiz.explain: Was made. The passive here is doing real work: it removes the person who made it.

quiz.prompt: The keys _____ under the mat, exactly where he said. (find)
quiz.explain: Keys is plural, so were, and find / found / found.

results: Clean run. You can turn a sentence around and you know when the doer is worth keeping.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at camp three before the rest of the descent.
Good first attempt. The third form is the part to read again.
